method: Kimi K3 read each design session and listed the moments where the design AI needed design knowledge (a need). Each need was embedded, matched to its 5 nearest cards, and Kimi graded whether those cards cover it: covered, partly (the topic exists but not the number or rule for that situation), or none. Uncovered and partly covered needs were clustered into themes with suggested cards.

themes.theme: Child Comfort, Session Length & Fatigue Limits
themes.why: The design AI repeatedly fails to give age-appropriate session durations, fatigue stop-signals, headset fit for small heads, hygiene between shared child users, and supervision rules. This is the single largest cluster and a safety-critical gap: wrong durations or missed discomfort signs directly harm young players.
examples: How should a first-time VR experience for a young child be onboarded: who wears and fits the headset, tutorial length, controller vs hand-tracking, and parent guidance role?
What session length is recommended for a 6-year-old's first VR experience, especially before bedtime, and what signs of fatigue or discomfort should end the session early?
What safety and comfort rules should a first-time 6-year-old MR player have: adult supervision, headset fit, session length, movement speed, and stopping signals?

themes.theme: Onboarding & First-Time-User Flow (Children, Novices, Older Adults)
themes.why: The AI consistently misses concrete onboarding sequences: passthrough-first entry, one-mechanic-at-a-time teaching, demo-then-copy scripts, sub-minute party onboarding, and fast restart loops. themes.why: The AI misses the mechanics that make same-room races fair and fun: synchronized starts, ghosting, lane assignment, tie-breaks, contested vs personal targets, paired physical actions, and leaderboard metrics. These are the social-competition rules that distinguish a race from parallel solo play.
examples: How do you make a parallel 'each player walks their own copy' race fair in MR: identical checkpoint spacing per copy, synchronized start, and a clear first-to-finish win condition?
For friends racing in one room, what start, ghosting, collision, lane-assignment, and tie-break rules keep the competition fair and socially fun?
How should competitive scoring work when several players race for the same limited set of targets in one shared space: contested vs personal targets, count-based vs time-based scoring?
